title: The Thief and His Mother
summary: A young boy stole a hornbook from his schoolfellow and brought it home to his mother. Instead of correcting him, she praised his cleverness and patted his head. Encouraged by her a...
full_text:
A young boy stole a hornbook from his schoolfellow and brought it home to his mother. Instead of correcting him, she praised his cleverness and patted his head. Encouraged by her approval, he stole a silver spoon from a neighbor, and she hid it with delight.

As the boy grew to manhood, his petty thefts expanded into violent highway robbery and murder. Eventually, he was captured by the king's soldiers and condemned to the gallows.

As he was led to the scaffold surrounded by a great crowd, his mother followed, weeping and tearing her hair. The condemned youth asked permission to whisper one last word in his mother's ear.

When she drew close, the youth clamped his teeth onto her earlobe and bit it clean off!

The crowd gasped in horror at the unnatural brutality. The youth turned to the crowd and cried with bitter tears: "Do not judge me alone! If this woman had struck my cheek when I first stole that little hornbook, I would not be standing beneath this gallows today; her praise has brought my ruin!"
moral: Neglecting to correct small faults in childhood breeds ruinous crimes in youth.

title: The Ass and the Wolf

full_text:
An ass grazing in a meadow saw a ravenous wolf approaching with bared fangs. Knowing he had no speed to outrun the beast, the ass immediately began limping with dramatic groans, dragging his hind leg through the clover.

The curious wolf paused and asked: "Why do you limp so pitifully, beast?"

"Alas, sir," wept the ass, "while leaping a hedge, a giant, jagged thorn pierced the sole of my hoof! I know you are going to eat me, but I beg you: pull out the thorn first, lest it pierce your throat and choke you while you feast upon my flank!"

The wolf thought this prudent advice. He stepped behind the ass, lifted the hoof, and bent his eyes close to search for the thorn.

In that instant, the ass kicked out with both hind hooves with thunderous force! The iron-hard hooves struck the wolf squarely in the mouth, shattering his teeth and splitting his jaw, while the ass galloped off to safety, laughing at the fallen predator.
moral: Sharp presence of mind in danger turns an enemy’s weapons into his own downfall.

title: The Buffoon and the Countryman

full_text:
A celebrated city buffoon drew immense crowds to the theater by mimicking the squealing of a pig beneath his cloak. He squeaked, grunted, and squealed so humorously that the audience cheered and awarded him the grand prize.

A simple countryman in the crowd stood up and declared that he would compete against the buffoon the following evening.

The next day, the theater was packed. The buffoon repeated his performance and received thunderous applause.

The countryman then stepped onto the stage, wrapped in a thick cloak. He pinched a real live piglet concealed beneath his arm, causing the animal to squeal and shriek with genuine pig cries.

The audience jeered and hissed, throwing rotten fruit and shouting: "Terrible! The buffoon sounds far more like a pig than you do!"

The countryman pulled the live piglet out from under his cloak and held it high above his head: "Behold, critics! It is not me you are hissing, but the pig himself! Your prejudice prefers a counterfeit to nature's own truth!"
moral: Prejudice blinds men to genuine truth in favor of celebrated counterfeits.

title: The Fox and the Woodcutter

full_text:
A fox, breathless and exhausted from a long pursuit by royal hounds, burst into a clearing where an honest woodcutter was chopping pine logs. The fox fell upon his knees and begged: "Have mercy, woodcutter! Hide me in your cottage, I implore you, or the hounds will tear me apart!"

The woodcutter pointed toward his rustic hut and promised to protect him. The fox dashed inside and crouched beneath a pile of dry faggots.

A moment later, the huntsmen arrived on foaming horses. "Woodcutter!" shouted the captain. "Did a fox pass this way?"

"No, I have seen no fox!" shouted the woodcutter with a loud, honest voice. But at the very same moment, he slyly pointed his thumb toward the door of his cottage, winking at the hunters.

The huntsmen, listening only to his words and ignoring his gesture, galloped past down the road.

When the danger had passed, the fox emerged from the hut and trotted off into the woods without uttering a single word of thanks.

"Where is your gratitude?" called the woodcutter indignantly. "I saved your skin, and you leave without a polite farewell!"

The fox turned around and replied: "I would have thanked you with all my heart if your fingers had agreed with your tongue, and if your deeds had not contradicted your speech!"
moral: Hypocrisy that swears faith with words while betraying with deeds is contemptible.

full_text:
A birdcatcher was busily spreading fine horsehair nets across a stubble field and scattering sweet millet seeds upon the ground to entice woodland birds.

A crest-lark perched upon a wild rose bush watched him from afar and asked curiously: "Good sir, what magnificent work are you engaged in with those ropes and pegs?"

The birdcatcher smiled warmly and replied: "I am laying the foundations of a grand, prosperous new city where all creatures may live in abundance and peace!"

With these words, the man retreated into the bushes.

The simple lark, captivated by the promise of a peaceful city and enticed by the scattered grain, fluttered down to feast. The moment his claws touched the seed, the snare snapped shut, tangling his delicate wings in the horsehair cords.

As the birdcatcher stepped forward to wring his neck, the lark wept in bitter despair: "Alas! If this is the kind of city you build, master builder, you will find very few citizens willing to inhabit it!"
moral: Beware the treacherous stranger who lays traps while pretending to build a city.

An elderly fisherman sat upon a stone pier casting his line into the sea all morning without success. At noon, his cork bobbed under, and he pulled up a tiny sprat no bigger than his thumb.

As the fisherman prepared to toss the tiny catch into his willow basket, the little fish opened his mouth and gasped:

"Have pity, fisherman! Look at how small I am—I am barely a single bite for a hungry man! Throw me back into the cool ocean waves! Let me swim and grow fat for another season; then you may catch me again and sell me at the harbor market for a silver coin!"

The old fisherman slipped the little fish into his creel, secured the wicker lid, and replied with a serene smile:

"I should be a fool indeed to surrender a small fish already in my basket on the doubtful chance of catching a larger one in the stormy future!"
moral: A small certainty in hand is worth far more than a grand promise in the future.

title: The Dog and the Shadow
summary: A dog crossing a brook with a juicy piece of meat in his mouth saw his reflection in the tranquil stream. Mistaking it for another dog carrying a larger prize, he snapped at the ph...
full_text:
On a bright morning in an ancient village, a butcher tossed a succulent, juicy bone with a tender cut of meat to a stray dog that had been waiting patiently outside his shop. Overjoyed with his good fortune, the dog clasped the prize tightly between his jaws. Rather than enjoying his meal in front of the barking neighborhood dogs who might demand a share, he decided to carry his treasure deep into the quiet woodland where he could feast in undisturbed peace.

Trotting proudly across the green meadows, he soon arrived at a clear mountain brook spanned by a narrow wooden footbridge. As he stepped onto the planks, he glanced down into the crystalline water below. To his utter astonishment, staring back at him from the tranquil depths was another dog—carrying what appeared to be an even larger, juicier, and more magnificent cut of meat!

Blinded by sudden envy and uncontrollable greed, the dog could not bear the thought of another creature having a finer feast than his own. Without pausing for a single moment of reflection, he snarled ferociously and snapped his jaws open to snatch the phantom prize from the water. In that very instant, his own meat slipped from his mouth, splashed into the rushing stream, and sank quickly to the gravelly bottom. As the rippling water dissolved the reflection, the foolish dog was left dripping wet, empty-mouthed, and thoroughly ashamed, realizing that in grasping at an illusion, he had surrendered his true feast.
moral: Grasping at a shadowy illusion sacrifices the real blessing in hand.

title: The Hawk and the Pigeons
summary: Pigeons, harassed by a kite, invited a hawk to be their protector. The hawk accepted, entered their dovecote, and slaughtered more pigeons in a single day than the kite had in a ye...
full_text:
High in the peaceful rafters of a rustic farm dovecote, a flock of white pigeons lived in constant dread. A fierce brown kite circled the skies above every afternoon, swooping down whenever a bird ventured into the open fields to forage for seeds. Though the kite managed to seize only a stray bird every few weeks, the pigeons lived in endless terror, shivering within the eaves and holding anxious assemblies to debate how they might secure their safety.

In their desperation, an elder dove proposed a bold measure: 'Let us appeal to the great hawk, the undisputed master of the high winds! He possesses mighty talons and terrifying speed; if we invite him into our dovecote to serve as our royal protector, the cowardly kite will never dare show his face in our valley again.' Blinded by fear, the flock hailed the suggestion with enthusiasm. They sent an emissary to the hawk’s mountain aerie, promising him an honored dwelling in their roost. Flattered and hungry, the fierce hawk eagerly accepted their petition and flew down into the dovecote with an imposing display of sharp talons.

No sooner was the hawk securely lodged within the narrow entrance of the roost than his predatory nature showed itself in all its fury. Barring the exit with his wide wings, he began slaughtering the helpless pigeons one by one, feasting upon more birds in a single morning than the kite had captured in an entire year! As the surviving pigeons huddled in the shadowy corners awaiting their doom, a dying dove wept in bitter remorse: 'Alas for our blind folly! In our eagerness to escape a minor annoyance, we have invited our greatest destroyer into our very home.' Too late did they learn that seeking the protection of a tyrant is a cure far deadlier than the affliction.
moral: Inviting a tyrant to protect you from a petty foe invites your own slaughter.

title: The Dove and the Crow
summary: A dove in a cage boasted of hatching many broods. A crow remarked: "Why do you boast, foolish mother? The more children you hatch, the more slaves you produce for your master!"...
full_text:
Inside the ornate courtyard of a wealthy merchant's villa, a pampered white dove lived inside an elaborate gilded wicker cage. Every morning, the master’s servants brought her fresh millet, clean spring water, and soft cotton for her nest, ensuring she was shielded from the cold winds and predators of the open world.

Proud of her quiet shelter, the dove sat beside her nest and began boasting loudly to the wild birds gathered on the courtyard eaves: "Look upon my fruitful nest! I have hatched four fine broods of fledglings this season alone, more than any wild bird in the entire district! Is there any mother under heaven more blessed and productive than I?"

A ragged wild crow, perched on the tiled roof of the stable, looked down through the wire bars with a gaze of sorrowful pity. "Why do you boast, foolish captive?" croaked the crow. "Every chick you bring forth into that cage will never know the freedom of soaring over mountain valleys or wheeling through the open sky. The more fledglings you hatch within your gilded bars, the more captives you provide to serve your master's amusement. To multiply children into servitude is no honor; true blessing lies in freedom, not in the abundance of one's chains."
moral: Multiplying children in captivity only multiplies the parent’s sorrow.
